Before you pull the trigger tomorrow, though—can you take a sick day or a mental health day first? ## 2

I understand why people are skeptical of big institutions and CGI, but you don't actually need NASA or satellite imagery to know the Earth is a sphere. People figured this out thousands of years before cameras existed.

For example, during a lunar eclipse, the Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, casting its shadow onto the lunar surface. That shadow is always a smooth, curved arc, no matter what time of night the eclipse happens or where the Moon is in the sky. If the Earth were a flat disk, you’d sometimes see an elongated oval or a thin slit depending on the angle. The only shape that casts a circular shadow from every possible direction is a sphere.

Or consider constellations: if you travel from Canada down to Chile, entirely new stars appear above the southern horizon while familiar northern stars sink out of sight. On a flat plane, everyone on Earth would see the exact same stars, just slightly closer or further away. 

Faking a digital photo is easy; coordinating millions of independent sailors, airline pilots, surveyors, and amateur stargazers across every continent for thousands of years to maintain a shared illusion is impossible.

## 3

To understand why the sky is blue, you first have to know two things: sunlight isn't purely white, and the air around us isn't empty space.

Light from the Sun looks white, but it's actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow combined. Each color travels through space as a wave. Red and orange light travel in long, lazy waves, while blue and violet light travel in short, choppy, energetic waves.

When that sunlight hits Earth, it runs into our atmosphere, which is packed with billions of tiny gas molecules—mostly nitrogen and oxygen. 

The long, lazy waves of red and yellow light are big enough to pass right past those tiny molecules without bumping into them much. But the short, choppy blue waves smash directly into the gas particles and bounce off them in every direction. Scientists call this **scattering**. 

When you look up during the day, you aren't looking at empty space; you’re looking at all those tiny blue waves that got knocked off course, ping-ponging across the entire atmosphere and down into your eyes.

窗外的雨下得又急又密，敲打在玻璃上，发出细碎而沉闷的声响。路灯昏黄的光晕在被雨水浸湿的柏油路上晕染开来，像融化在水里的油彩。偶尔有车辆飞驰而过，轮胎撕开积水，溅起半人高的水花，转瞬又重归寂静。冷风顺着窗缝渗进屋内，带来泥土与青草混合的微凉潮气。房间里只亮着一盏暖光台灯，在这片朦胧的水汽中，整座城市仿佛都随着这场夜雨，慢慢沉入了深沉的梦乡。
